turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome. What brings you into the clinic today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, doctor. Thank you. Well, it’s a bit of a long story, but I suppose the main thing that finally made me pick up the phone and make this appointment... well, you see, I’m a secondary school teacher. I've been teaching for decades, and you’d really think by the time you reach sixty, you’d have learned how to just sit still, wouldn't you? 

But what brought me in is that I just keep getting up. Constantly. If we're in a staff meeting, and everyone else is perfectly fine just sitting there in their chairs, paying attention, I’ll suddenly feel this... this need to stand up. I’ll make up some little excuse, like I suddenly need to refill my coffee, or I'll go check a handout on the back table, or I’ll just walk to the back of the room to stand. And the ridiculous thing is, nothing is really urgent! I don't actually need the coffee. 

And it’s not just at school, it happens at home, too. We’ll be sitting down for dinner, just a nice quiet meal where everyone is seated, and I just can’t stay planted in my chair. I’ll pop up to get a napkin, sit back down, then pop right back up to check the kitchen counter even though the food is already on the plates. My husband gets so exasperated, and I want to stay seated, I really do, but it’s like my body just decides it’s time to move. Before I even consciously think about it, I’m already out of my chair. It’s terribly embarrassing, especially at my age and in my profession, to be the only one who can't just sit through a standard thirty-minute meeting without wandering around...

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly describes constantly getting up from their chair during staff meetings and dinners when remaining seated is expected.

turns.patient_response:
Oh, you mean like a specific feeling in my legs? Like an ache or a creeping sensation or something like that? No, no, it’s really nothing like that at all. 

It's not an uncomfortable physical sensation in my calves or thighs or anywhere else. It’s not a cramp or a tickle or a numbness. It’s more of just... an overwhelming, full-body urge, I suppose? Or not even an urge, just this absolute certainty that I need to be vertical right that very second. It’s like my brain just sends a signal that says, "Alright, time to be up now!" and before I can even properly process it, my hands are already on the armrests and I'm pushing myself up out of the seat. 

I don't feel a creeping feeling in my legs at all, it's just that my legs are the things that have to do the work to get me out of the chair, if you see what I mean. Like just yesterday, for instance, I was grading papers—just a small stack of year ten history essays, nothing too taxing, really, just covering the Industrial Revolution—and my legs felt perfectly fine, completely normal, but I still had to get up and walk around the kitchen island three times before I could sit back down and read the next essay. My husband was reading the paper and just sighed, but I couldn't help it. So, no, it’s definitely not a weird feeling in the legs themselves, just a general... well, a need to not be sitting anymore. I just have to be moving.

  "intent": "Determine whether these symptoms of restlessness have been present since childhood.",
  "question": "Did you experience this kind of restlessness when you were a child?"
turns.patient_response:
Oh, goodness, yes. Yes, I absolutely did. It’s funny you ask that, because I was actually just thinking about this the other day when I was going through some old boxes in the attic... looking for some old photo albums, actually, for my daughter's anniversary, but I got completely sidetracked. 

My mother kept absolutely everything, you know how mothers from that generation were. Every single report card from the time I was in primary school was tucked away in this old biscuit tin. And looking back at them, well... it was quite eye-opening, really. The teachers always wrote the loveliest things about my intelligence—they'd say I was "bright," or "quick to catch on"—but there was always, without fail, a little note at the bottom. Always! Something along the lines of, "She is a bright girl, but she simply cannot stay in her seat." Or they'd mention how I had a terrible time waiting my turn to speak or participate. 

And I remember... oh, I must have been... well, definitely before I was ten years old. I remember my mother used to joke with her friends about it when they'd come over for tea. We had these dreadful wooden desks at my school, the heavy ones with the little grooves for your pencils. And my mother would laugh and tell everyone that I must have worn a literal path in the floorboards between my desk and the pencil sharpener! 

Because I was always getting up to sharpen my pencil. Constantly. Even if it was perfectly sharp, I'd just grind it down to an absolute nub just so I'd have a reason to stand up and walk to the front of the room where the sharpener was bolted to the wall. It was just an excuse, you see, exactly like the coffee in my staff meetings now. I just needed to be up. I mean, back then, in the sixties, they didn't really think much of it, especially for girls. They just thought I was a bit of a fidget or highly strung. But it’s exactly the same feeling now as it was then. It’s quite silly when you think about it, isn't it? A sixty-year-old woman doing the exact same thing she did at age eight, just swapping the pencil sharpener for a coffee pot, but... well, there it is. The urge has always been exactly the same.

turns.doctor_question: Outside of needing to move around, do you often have trouble keeping your focus on tasks or conversations?
turns.patient_response:
Trouble keeping my focus? Oh, no, no, not at all. It’s actually quite the opposite, really. My mind is perfectly sharp, thank goodness! 

It’s funny you ask that, because my husband, Arthur—he’s always saying I have a memory like an elephant and a mind like a steel trap when it comes to conversations. If we're talking, I am right there with you, completely engaged. I don't drift off or start daydreaming. Like, just this past weekend, we had our neighbors over, the Pearsons, and Margaret was going on and on in absolute excruciating detail about her new kitchen renovation—she’s putting in these quartz countertops that cost an absolute fortune, which I think is a bit silly, but anyway—she was talking for a solid hour, and I heard every single word. I didn't lose the thread of the conversation once! 

Now, mind you, I might have gotten up to offer everyone more tea three different times, and I certainly rearranged the coasters on the coffee table while she was talking, but my brain was completely locked in. I knew exactly what she was saying the entire time. 

And it’s the exact same with my tasks. As a teacher, you simply have to be able to focus, don't you? When I sit down to grade those history essays I mentioned, or when I'm reading a really thick book—I love historical biographies, I just finished a massive one on Queen Victoria last month—I can read through them with absolute clarity. I don't lose my place or forget what I'm doing or get distracted by the birds outside. The problem is just that my body wants to be doing the reading while pacing the hallway! 

So, no, my mind doesn't wander off... I don't have any trouble paying attention to things at all. I can focus on a book or a chat perfectly fine. It's really just the physical need to be up and about that’s the bother.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient mentions getting up multiple times during a conversation and wanting to pace the hallway while reading.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly notes a physical need to be up and about.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly denies having trouble paying attention to tasks or conversations, stating they can focus perfectly fine.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient denies drifting off during conversations, stating they remain completely engaged and hear every word.
